Scouting Summary

Common themes

  • Right Medium, averaging 126.7 kph (up to 136.7).
  • Typical length is 6-7m (their good length); median 6.8 m.
  • Stock ball is a good length outside off, seaming both ways, swinging both ways, hitting the top of off (30% of deliveries).
  • Round the wicket to LHB 56% · over the wicket to RHB (round 0%).
  • Round the wicket he shifts his pitching line from wide of 6th to 6th stump.
  • Across an over he hammers a repeatable length, banging it in more as the over goes on.

Biggest threats

  • Most dangerous length is Full (6 wkts, 1.8% adjusted strike).
  • Danger pitching line: Wide of 6th (over the wicket).
  • Takes 28% of wickets pitching a good length wide outside off.
  • Beats the bat 6.9% of tracked balls (false-shot 17.3%).
  • Gets you caught behind more than most — 80% of his wickets (1.2× the typical rate for this type).
  • 65% of catches are behind the wicket (keeper / slips / gully); most often to keeper, slip: 2nd, point: regulation.

Areas to exploit

  • Concedes most runs pitching a good length wide outside off (20% of runs).
  • Short ball: 18% of deliveries, economy 4.3 — 5 wkts from 237 short balls.
  • Away from full, the wicket threat drops off — look to score in the less-productive lengths.
  • Most of the runs off them leak square/through the off side (48%) — their main scoring release.

Solid line = career, dotted = last 3 years (where enough recent balls). Percentile within same-type peers (grey = the peer distribution, line = this bowler). Release/crease vs hand × pace/spin; movement/speed/repeatability vs pace/spin. Release & speed are modern-era (2017+ / partial). Crease variation = how much he moves his release point sideways across the crease from ball to ball (within his main angle): a high percentile = he varies where he lets the ball go a lot, a low percentile = he releases from the same spot every ball. Repeatability = length consistency over his stock-length band (2–11 m, so deliberate yorkers and bouncers don't count as poor control): a high percentile = tighter, more metronomic lengths than peers; a low percentile = he varies his length more. A marker at the very edge = he sits beyond the typical peer range on that trait.

Sequencing & Over Construction

Metronomic — hammers the same length repeatedly, little to feast on (length spread ±1.6 m; more repeatable than 90% of pace bowlers); tends to bang it in later in the over (short 2%→7% by the 5th–6th ball); and holds the same crease position through the over.
Across 22 dismissals, his wicket ball is close in length and pace to the delivery before it — he builds pressure with repetition, not a big change-up.
